title: CSS icons: icon fonts, SVG, and accessible usage
learningObjectives: Explain css icons: icon fonts, svg, and accessible usage and its role in modern CSS.
Write valid CSS syntax and predict the computed result.
Choose the technique appropriate to a real interface requirement.
Identify common implementation, accessibility, and browser-support pitfalls.
Test and explain the behaviour using browser developer tools.

understand.concept: Icons can be included as inline SVG, external SVG files, icon fonts, or component libraries. Icon fonts map glyphs to font characters, while SVG describes vector shapes and can provide precise scalable graphics. Choose an approach based on licensing, performance, theming, accessibility, and build constraints. A decorative icon should be hidden from assistive technology when adjacent text already names the action. An icon-only control needs an accessible name, a visible focus state, and a sufficiently large target. Do not rely on a private-use font glyph without loading the matching font.
understand.whyItMatters: Icons improve scanning only when they are recognizable and accessible. Poorly loaded fonts, unlabeled icon buttons, and unlicensed assets can make an interface confusing or fragile.
understand.analogy: An icon is a visual shorthand; text is the label that confirms what the shorthand means.
understand.analogyLimit: Icons are not universally understood, and decorative appearance cannot replace accessible names or clear interaction feedback.

explain.narrative: Compare a text-labelled SVG icon with an icon-only button. Review what happens if an icon font fails to load and why the control still needs an accessible name.

examples.code: <button type="button" aria-label="Open settings"><svg aria-hidden="true" viewBox="0 0 24 24" width="24" height="24"><path d="M12 3v18M3 12h18" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/></svg></button>
examples.explanation: The button has an accessible name and the decorative SVG is hidden from the accessibility tree. The example path is a simple plus shape; replace it with a suitable licensed settings icon in a real product.
examples.expectedOutput: An icon-only button announced as Open settings.

examples.explanation: The icon is decorative because the adjacent visible text names the action. A production icon font should be loaded from a trusted, licensed asset and should have a sensible fallback.
examples.expectedOutput: A Save item button with a decorative star glyph.

practise.guidedTask: Implement a small icon set using inline SVG or a licensed icon library. Test the interface with the icon font disabled and with a screen reader; every action must remain understandable.
practise.independentTask: Compare SVG sprites, inline SVG, icon fonts, and a component library against bundle size, caching, licensing, styling, and accessibility requirements. Record the chosen trade-off.
hints: Use aria-hidden="true" for a decorative icon when equivalent text is present.
Give icon-only buttons an accessible name such as aria-label.
Check licensing and font loading; never assume a glyph will render on every device.

questions.prompt: Which technique gives an icon-only button an accessible name?
options: A clear aria-label or equivalent accessible text
questions.answer: A clear aria-label or equivalent accessible text
questions.explanation: The control needs a programmatic name that explains its action.

questions.prompt: When is aria-hidden="true" appropriate on an icon?
options: When the icon is decorative and equivalent text already names the action
When the icon is the only label
questions.answer: When the icon is decorative and equivalent text already names the action
questions.explanation: Decorative content should not create duplicate or meaningless announcements.

questions.prompt: What is one advantage of SVG icons?
options: They are vector graphics that scale cleanly
They automatically load every icon font
questions.answer: They are vector graphics that scale cleanly
questions.explanation: SVG scales well and can be styled, but accessibility still needs deliberate handling.

questions.prompt: What should be checked before using an icon library?
options: Whether it removes the need for text labels
questions.explanation: Third-party assets introduce licensing and delivery considerations.

questions.prompt: What should happen if an icon font fails to load?
options: The action should remain understandable and operable
questions.answer: The action should remain understandable and operable
questions.explanation: Text labels and accessible names keep controls meaningful even if decorative assets fail.
